name: metapool
workload: Construction and reserve() of mtp::vault (pool-backed dynamic array) vs std::vector (std::allocator/ptmalloc) and std::pmr::vector (pmr pool + monotonic_buffer_resource), across element counts.
claimed_speedup: up to ~1300x faster construction/reserve than std::vector (std::allocator); up to ~3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector (pool resource)
compiler_and_flags: clang 20.1.8; -O3 -march=native -fstrict-aliasing -flto
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U, Arch Linux kernel 6.15.8, glibc 2.42 (ptmalloc), 64GB DDR5
tradeoffs: Compile-time fixed pool layout (metaset) must be tuned per workload; no general fallback beyond configured strides; header-only but requires C++23; cannot grow arbitrarily beyond the preallocated arena without a reset.
caveats: The ~1300x figure comes from a narrow construction+reserve microbenchmark (bypassing malloc/realloc growth entirely), not sustained alloc/free churn; the ~3.5x-vs-pmr figure is more representative of general use. New project (created Aug 2025), 37 stars, no independent third-party verification found.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ pool allocator faster than std::allocator benchmark github'

name: Hoard
baseline: Solaris default allocator, Ptmalloc (glibc malloc backing operator new/delete)
workload: Uniprocessor and multiprocessor (1-14 way Sun Enterprise 5000) allocation-intensive benchmarks: threadtest, shbench, Larson server simulation, active/passive false-sharing tests, BEMengine PDE solver, Barnes-Hut n-body solver, plus single-threaded espresso/Ghostscript/LRUsim/p2c.
claimed_speedup: Up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator and up to 18x over the next-best allocator (Ptmalloc) at 14 processors (paper abstract); threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; BEMengine 10.6% faster than Solaris allocator uniprocessor
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ at -O6 (Sun Workshop C++ compiler 5.0 used only for Barnes-Hut)
hardware: Sun Enterprise 5000, 2GB RAM, 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC CPUs, 4MB L2 cache, Solaris 7
stars_or_usage: 1.25k stars; historically used by AOL, Cisco, SAP, Reuters, RBC and others per README; standard allocator option in SPEC CPU2006
tradeoffs: Multi-heap design trades some memory for scalability (bounded blowup, not zero); link-time/LD_PRELOAD drop-in malloc replacement, not a std::allocator template adapter; per-processor heap hashing can cause heap/thread collisions.
caveats: Primary quantitative evidence is a peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper run on 26-year-old hardware (UltraSPARC/Solaris 7) against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era, not a modern libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL build; no current reproduction with stated modern compiler/flags/hardware was found this session, so capped at Tier B rather than A. The GitHub repo itself is actively maintained in 2026 as a drop-in malloc replacement, and Hoard is also included (as 'hd') in the independent daanx/mimalloc-bench suite, though that page's results are chart images only, not text numbers.
found_via: GitHub: found via daanx/mimalloc-bench README allocator list ('hd' = Hoard); followed citation to the ASPLOS 2000 paper

name: arena-allocator (ShortAlloc)
baseline: operator new/delete (GNU/glibc malloc via std::vector's default std::allocator)
workload: std::vector<TestClass>::emplace_back of 100 objects of sizes 8B-8KB, using a stack-backed bump-pointer Arena + ShortAlloc STL allocator vs the default heap allocator, measured on QuickBench (AWS-hosted).
claimed_speedup: Stack/arena allocator 2.2x-4.4x faster for objects up to 512B, and 93x-230x faster for 1KB-8KB objects (crossing glibc's mmap threshold)
hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool; CPU model and load unstated (README includes explicit disclaimer that absolute QuickBench timings are unreliable)
stars_or_usage: 9 stars; featured in a Hacker News 'Show HN' post
tradeoffs: Bump allocator: cannot free individual objects out of order, only the whole arena at once (or most-recent-first); backed by a fixed-size std::array, so capacity is bounded by the configured arena size; not thread-safe.
caveats: Compiler and optimization flags are not stated, and several ratios (93x-230x) exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, coinciding with crossing glibc's mmap allocation threshold (a known artifact of that one size range, not a general allocator speed claim) -- capped at Tier C rather than A. QuickBench's own disclaimer says absolute durations on its shared AWS pool are 'meaningless' beyond relative comparison. No LICENSE file in the repo, so usability is 'reference' only, not 'copyable'.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'arena allocator C++ github faster than operator new' -> Hacker News 'Show HN: C++ Arena Allocator That's 200x+ Faster Than GNU Malloc'

name: CRoaring (Roaring Bitmaps)
baseline: uncompressed bitset with the same word-array representation as std::bitset/std::vector<bool> (the paper's own portable C reimplementation, 'cbitset', is used in the benchmark rather than literally std::bitset or std::vector<bool>)
workload: 8 realistic integer-set datasets (CensusInc, CensusInc-sorted, Census1881, Census1881-sorted, Weather, Weather-sorted, Wikileaks, Wikileaks-sorted; 200 sets each, universe sizes 200K-4.3M): sequential iteration/cardinality, random-access membership queries at n/4, n/2, 3n/4, and 199 pairwise intersections/unions/differences/symmetric differences between successive sets. Reported as CPU cycles per input value.
claimed_speedup: Mixed by dataset and operation. Intersections (Table 7a, cycles/value): bitset 19.5 vs Roaring 0.090 on Census1881 (~217x faster, derived from page data); bitset 33.0 vs Roaring 0.140 on Census1881-sorted (~236x, derived from page data); bitset 26.4 vs Roaring 1.43 on Wikileaks (~18x, derived from page data). But on CensusInc/CensusInc-sorted/Weather, the plain bitset is FASTER than Roaring (e.g. bitset 0.130 vs Roaring 0.220-0.380 cycles/value on CensusInc, i.e. bitset ~1.7-2.9x faster there). Random-access membership queries (Table 6): plain bitset wins on every dataset (2.4-3.7 cycles vs Roaring's 17-77 cycles). Memory (Table 4): Roaring uses far less than an uncompressed bitset on sparse data, e.g. 2.60 vs 524 bits/value on Census1881, 0.34 vs 11.4 bits/value on Weather-sorted.
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 5.4, compiled with -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.4 GHz, 32KB L1d, 256KB L2/core, 8MB L3), 32GB DDR4-2133 dual-channel, single-threaded, Turbo Boost disabled, timed with rdtsc, results reproducible within 5%
stars_or_usage: 1,887 stars; used by Apache Doris, ClickHouse, Alibaba Tair, Redpanda, YDB, StarRocks
tradeoffs: Roaring wins decisively on memory and on set-algebra over sparse/clustered 32-bit integer sets, but loses to a plain uncompressed bitset on random-access membership queries (bitset has roughly an order of magnitude lower latency) and can lose on set-algebra for dense/small-universe datasets. Targets dynamic sparse 32-bit integer sets, not fixed-size dense bit flags, so it is not a general drop-in for std::bitset<N> or std::vector<bool>.
caveats: The paper's 'bitset' baseline is the authors' own portable C library ('cbitset', github.com/lemire/cbitset: ceil(n/64) 64-bit words, no processor-specific optimizations), not literally std::bitset or std::vector<bool> from a standard library implementation, though it is representationally identical to both, so baseline_in_list is recorded true with reduced confidence. Results are strongly dataset- and operation-dependent; the entry reports both wins and losses rather than a single headline number. Authors of the paper are also the library's maintainers (Lemire et al., published in Software: Practice and Experience, 2018), but code, compiler, flags, and CPU model are all public and stated, satisfying Tier A methodology regardless of who ran it.

name: plf::bitset (plf_bitsets)
workload: Full bitset test-suite exercised in a loop (set/reset/shift/index/etc.); separately, set_range/reset_range on a 128000-bit bitset over 10000 randomly chosen ranges per run.
claimed_speedup: Release (O2, AVX2): 24% (GCC)/20% (MSVC) faster overall test suite; 34,652%/67,612% faster set_range/reset_range; ~101%/98% faster left/right shift (GCC), 35%/22% (MSVC); 6%/204% faster set(pos,val); 3%/0% faster operator[]. Debug builds show much larger gaps (up to 428,127%/750,726% for set_range/reset_range).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2 (nuwen mingw) and MSVC 2022; release build: O2, AVX2, C++23
hardware: Intel i7-9750H, Windows 10 (safe mode)
tradeoffs: plf::bitset omits std::bitset's from-string/from-ulong constructors; adds set_range/reset_range, range-based any/all/none/count, an allocation-free XOR swap, index-bounds-checking via a template flag, and a user-supplied-buffer variant (plf::bitsetb) not present in std::bitset.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project author's own numbers), not independently reproduced, though methodology (compiler, flags, hardware) and full benchmark source are published. The extreme set_range/reset_range percentages (up to ~677x) largely reflect that std::bitset has no native ranged-set primitive (callers must loop bit-by-bit), so this is partly an algorithmic-complexity win (O(1) words vs O(n) bits) rather than a raw constant-factor speedup; the overall test-suite numbers (~20-24%) are the more representative figure for general use. Licensed under 'Computing For Good License v1.01' (zlib-like but with additional ethical-use-restriction clauses 4a-4e), which is not OSI-approved due to those field-of-use restrictions, so usability is 'reference' rather than 'copyable'.

name: atomic_queue
workload: SPSC round-trip ping-pong: 2 threads exchange a 4-byte int counter 1,000,000 times via two queue instances (lowest-contention case); also an N-producer/N-consumer throughput scalability test moving 1,000,000 messages through one queue, run across AMD Ryzen 5950X, Ryzen 5825U, Intel i9-9900KS and Intel Xeon Gold 6132.
claimed_speedup: AtomicQueue mean round-trip latency 42ns vs std::mutex 320ns on Ryzen 5950X (~7.6x lower); OptimistAtomicQueue 33ns (~9.7x lower). At 1-producer/1-consumer throughput: AtomicQueue 142.7M msg/s vs std::mutex 4.1M msg/s (~34x); OptimistAtomicQueue reports up to ~1.23B msg/s in the same 1P/1C cell, which is an implausible outlier (see caveats).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-14.2.0 (primary systems; gcc-8.4.0 on legacy i9-9900KS/Xeon Gold systems); Makefile release flags: -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -std=c++14 -falign-functions=64 -DNDEBUG
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X and Ryzen 5825U (KDE Neon/Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, mitigations=off); legacy: Intel i9-9900KS (Kubuntu 18.04) and Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (RHEL 6.10)
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; packaged in Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Fixed capacity set at compile/construction time (ring buffer, no heap growth); no OS-blocking wait, only busy-spin (push/pop can't sleep, unsuitable for non-latency-critical code that wants to yield the CPU); atomic-element variants reserve a NIL sentinel value that must never be pushed; value-semantics only (copies/moves elements, no in-place references).
caveats: The 1P/1C throughput cell for OptimistAtomicQueue (~1.23B msg/s, stdev ~135M) is far above what its own 42/33ns latency numbers would imply and is almost certainly a measurement/compiler-hoisting artifact of the fully uncontended, dependency-free loop rather than a sustained rate; treat the 7.6-9.7x latency figures as the solid claim and discount the >200x throughput figure. Throughput scaling is also non-monotonic across some thread counts (e.g. std::mutex briefly outperforms AtomicQueue at exactly 2 threads on the 5950X), which the author's own charts show and do not hide.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "atomic queue" --sort stars (seed-query variation of 'lock-free queue benchmark vs std::mutex std::queue'); opened repo README which links to the benchmarks.html shootout page
